Kyrgyz Som Plunges Amid Currency Crisis, Businesses Face Mounting Pressure

BISHKEK – Kyrgyzstan is grappling with a severe currency crisis that has seen the som lose nearly 40% of its value against the US dollar since mid-April, sparking widespread economic disruption and raising fears of broader instability.

Official data released by the National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic on Thursday showed the som trading at a historic low of 141.2 to the dollar, compared to 101.3 just six weeks ago. The collapse has triggered sharp increases in the prices of imported goods, fuel, and basic foodstuffs, while business confidence has tumbled.

"The sudden depreciation of the som has created significant uncertainty for our members," said Nurlan Joldoshev, president of the Kyrgyz Chamber of Commerce and Industry. "Many small and medium-sized enterprises rely on imported inputs, and now their costs have soared."

The currency’s slide began after a surprise interest rate cut by the central bank on April 18, intended to stimulate growth amid sluggish post-pandemic recovery. However, the move sparked capital outflows and stoked fears over the country's sizable foreign debt obligations.

"We are seeing significant pressure on the foreign reserves," acknowledged Aisuluu Bekbolotova, deputy governor of the National Bank, in a televised address. "We are committed to stabilizing the currency, but external factors have complicated our efforts."

Kyrgyzstan’s reliance on remittances and imports has magnified the crisis. According to the State Statistics Committee, remittances—mainly from migrant workers in Russia—fell by 18% in May compared to the previous year, as Russia’s own economy slowed. Meanwhile, approximately 60% of Kyrgyzstan’s consumer goods are imported, with prices for staples such as flour, vegetable oil, and sugar rising by as much as 35% since mid-April, according to the Bishkek Retailers’ Association.

"The shelves are full, but customers can’t afford to buy," said Bakyt Akmatov, director of the Ak-Ordo Retail Group. "We’re seeing a real squeeze on household budgets."

Exporters, however, report some benefit from the weaker som. "Our wool and textile products are more competitive abroad, but higher input costs eat into any gains," noted Zhibek Saparova, head of the Kyrgyz Exporters’ Union.

Analysts warn that unless confidence is restored, the crisis could deepen. "Without decisive action—including possible emergency support from international partners—the risk of hyperinflation and a broader economic downturn is rising," said Timur Kadyrov, senior economist at Central Asia Insights.

The government has pledged to unveil a stabilization plan in the coming days, but for many businesses and households, relief cannot come soon enough.
